replication.published: directional ablation sharply lowers refusal on harmful prompts in 13 chat models (Arditi et al. Fig. 1)
replication.ours: refusal on 64 harmful test prompts: 86% [75, 92] → 0% [0, 6] (random direction: 84% [74, 91]; Wilson 95% CIs)
replication.criterion: ablation cuts refusal by ≥ 50 points while the random direction changes it by < 15

replication.claim: Adding the direction makes the model refuse harmless requests
replication.published: activation addition induces refusal on harmless instructions (§3)
replication.ours: refusal on 64 harmless prompts: 6% [2, 15] → 98% [92, 100] (random direction: 6% [2, 15]; Wilson 95% CIs)
replication.criterion: addition raises refusal by ≥ 50 points while the random direction raises it by < 15

replication.claim: Control: a label-shuffled direction neither removes nor induces refusal
replication.published: the refusal effect is specific to the harmful − harmless direction
replication.ours: shuffled-label direction: harmful refusal 86% [75, 92] → 94% [85, 98] when ablated; harmless refusal 6% [2, 15] → 2% [0, 8] when added (Wilson 95% CIs)
replication.post_hoc: stronger control added after the methods review

replication.claim: Confirmatory: removing refusal leaves fluent text, not degeneration
replication.published: ablated models comply with harmful requests while staying coherent (Arditi et al., §4)
replication.ours: median NLL per token (tokens 6–40, under the unmodified model): ablated harmful completions 1.37 vs harmless baseline 0.51; median distinct-3-gram ratio 1.00 vs 1.00 (no text stored)
replication.criterion: NLL ≤ harmless + 1.0 nat and distinct-3 ≥ 0.8 × harmless (pre-stated 2026-11-28)
